title: Wolf-Rayet 124 (NIRCam and MIRI composite image)
caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 124, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: WR 124 · constellation Sagitta · about 15000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Webb ERO Production Team

recognition.text: Official ESA/Webb press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A large, bright star blazes at the centre with Webb's characteristic diffraction spikes, surrounded by a clumpy cloud that is thicker above and below than at the sides and turns yellow closer to the star. This is Wolf-Rayet 124, or WR 124, a luminous, hot, ageing massive star, in a combined near- and mid-infrared view.

The cloud is gas and dust thrown off by the star, stretching 10 light-years across. Its structure is a record of past episodes of mass loss. Instead of smooth shells, it formed through random, lopsided ejections.

Bright clumps look like tadpoles swimming toward the star, their tails blown back by the stellar wind. The two instruments worked together, with NIRCam balancing the star's glare against the fainter gas and dust while MIRI revealed the nebula's structure. Background stars and galaxies peek through the gaps.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.21 x 2.18 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 9.6 × 9.5 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI. Red is assigned to 4.44, 4.7, 12.8 and 18 microns, green to 2.1, 3.35 and 11.3 microns, and blue to 0.9, 1.5 and 7.7 microns.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the spikes around the star are an artefact of the telescope, not something in space.

explore: The star's spikes are not real features of WR 124. They arise from the way the telescope itself is built, and they are a signature of Webb's images.
alt: A large bright star with diffraction spikes at the centre, surrounded by a clumpy cloud, yellow near the star, with more material above and below, and background stars.
